Practical No: 1                                                                                                                    Introduction to Analytical Chemistry

Analytical chemistry is a science field evolving and adapting methods, devices and strategy for obtaining information about chemical composition, structure and energy state of substances. Goals of analytical chemistry: to detect chemical elements, which compose particular substance?
Qualitative analysis to determine the ratios of different elements in investigative substance
Quantitative analysis various substances differ from each other by composition, structure, physical and chemical properties. Most of properties can be used to learn about qualities, which distinguish substance from others.
These qualities are analytical signals
Methods of analysis are based on obtaining analysis signals and measurement of intensity of signals. According to action, which gives analytic signal, methods of analysis are divided into physical and chemical instrumental methods. They are employed in both in qualitative and quantitative analysis.
Chemical methods of analysis methods based on chemical interaction of atoms, molecules and ions. These methods are employed to detect characterize chemical properties of element or ion. Methods of chemical analysis can be divided according the type of chemical reaction, rate of chemical reaction and advisability (gravimetry, titrimetry, gas analysis, kinetic methods of analysis).
Physical methods are based on different parameters of substance radioactivity, electromagnetic properties, and radiation.
Also there are:
Biological methods based on use of biologically active substances and biological systems.
Biochemical method when substances of biological origin are investigated with chemical methods.
Analysis of chemical composition of substance proceeds by following steps:
    1. Choosing a sample; preparation of sample for analysis
    2. Extraction of component to investigate, purification; choosing method and scheme of analysis
    3. Disruption or solving of sample
    4. Separation and concentration
    5. Measurement of physical properties of sample, chemical reagent or product of chemical reaction
    6. Calculation of analysis data
    7. Estimation of results reliability.
Terminologies:
The sample is a material that we wish to analyze and also has a statistical meaning. The analyte is the substance or element in the sample whose presence or concentration we wish to determine. The matrix is other components of the sample other than the analyte.
The Analytical Process
Every scientist requires an understanding of analytical science so that the data produced fit the purpose. Analytical science can be considered as the science of problem solving. As can be seen in Figure, analytical science is a process rather than an end in itself:
• The technical approach to solving the problem requires the analyst to consider the analytical information, required level of accuracy, the cost, timing, availability of instruments and facilities before selecting the method.
• Knowledge and practical skills start with sampling. Without a representative sample, the results from the time consuming analysis are of little use. This is followed by the sample treatment to produce the analyte into suitable form for detection/measurement by the selected analytical technique. This may involve dissolution, separation of the analyte from the sample matrix or converting the analyte to another form.
• Interpretative skills are essential to determine the significance of the analytical results and their relevance in solving the original problem.

Q1: What is chemical analysis?
Chemical analysis includes any aspect of chemical characterization, starting from collection of
sample, extraction, sample preparation, instrumental analysis to statistical evaluation of collected
data.

Q2: Define complementary color?
When white light falls upon a sample, either reflection or absorption takes place. If only a
portion of the light is absorbed, the color of the sample is determined by the reflected light (is
called Complementary Colors).

Q3: Function of hollow cathode lamp?
HCL is a vacuumed Tube bearing Cylindrical cathode And some noble gas at very low pressure.
It generates photons of particular metal for which cathode is made.

Q4: Why transition metals and organic molecules show color?
Transition metals are colored because of d-d transitions while organic Molecules are colored
because of conjugation.

Q8: Note on UV spectroscopy?
UV spectroscopy, specifically UV-Vis spectroscopy, is an analytical technique that measures the
absorption of ultraviolet (UV) and visible (Vis) light by various substances. This method
provides valuable insights into the molecular structures and concentrations of chemicals within a
sample.

Principle:
When UV or Visible light is absorbed by a substance, the electrons in the molecule move from
their ground states to higher energy levels. Different molecules have unique absorption patterns
depending on their electronic configurations.

Instrument & its components:
The instrument used in this technique is UV spectrophotometer and has following components:

Light source

Monochromator

Sample compartment

Detector

Readout Device

Beer-Lambert law:
Absorption of light is directly proportional to both the concentration of the absorbing substance
and the path length of the light through the sample. Mathematically, this relationship is expressed
as:

A= ε*b*C
Where

A represents the absorbance,

ε is the molar absorptivity ,
C denotes the concentration, and

b stands for the path length.

(Note: It’s your choice whether you write Beer-Lambert law or just write till components.
You can also write applications of UV spectroscopy instead of Beer-Lambert law)

Q9: Note on ICP-OES?
ICP/OES stands for Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy. It is a type of
atomic emission spectroscopy.

In this technique, atomization source is changed to inductive coupled plasma. Temperature of
plasma can reach up to 10,000 K. Risk of chemical interference is low. 70 elements can be
determined to ppb (parts per billion) level.

Working of ICP:
The sample is prepared in liquid form as in case of FAAS (Flame Atomic Absorption
Spectroscopy).

Sample is injected through nebulizer at 0.5 to 1.5 mL/min.

The emitted spectral lines pass through monochromoator.
The separation in MS is on the basis of mass to charge ratio.

Q10: Importance of oxidation in chemical reactions?
Oxidation is defined in terms of loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, or an
increase in oxidation number.

Oxidation reactions are essential in chemistry, influencing organic synthesis by creating
functional groups essential for drugs and materials. In natural processes like photosynthesis,
oxidation is vital for energy production in plants. These reactions play a crucial role in redox
titrations for analytical purposes. Oxidation contributes to chemical synthesis, enabling the
creation of diverse compounds and innovative materials. In daily life, oxidation affects food
spoilage and wastewater treatment, while in combustion, it powers energy production.

Additionally, oxidation is integral to cellular respiration, extracting energy from nutrients.
Overall, these reactions are crucial, driving advancements in biology and technology.

Q11: Define solid phase extraction and its purpose in sample preparation for
chromatographic analysis.
Solid phase extraction is a sample preparation process by which compounds that are dissolved or
suspended in liquid mixture are separated from other compounds in the mixture according to
their physical and chemical properties.

Q. No. 1: A student of analytical chemistry is tasked with weighing 9g of NaCl
in the laboratory. Describe step- By-step how the student ensures precise
measurement and safety throughout the experiment, detailing each
Precautionary measure and instrument used.

Answer:

To weigh 9g of NaCl in the laboratory, the student should follow these steps to ensure precision
and safety:

   1. Preparation and Safety:
          o Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as a lab coat,
              safety goggles, and gloves to prevent contact with the chemical.
          o Ensure the weighing area is clean and free from contaminants to avoid inaccurate
              readings.
   2. Instrument Setup:
          o Use a top-loading balance or analytical balance for precise measurement.
          o Calibrate the balance if needed or ensure it is already calibrated.
          o Place the balance on a stable, vibration-free surface to avoid disturbances during
              weighing.
   3. Selection of Weighing Container:
          o Use a clean, dry weighing dish or beaker to hold the NaCl. Ensure the container
              is appropriate for the balance being used.
   4. Taring the Balance:
          o Place the weighing container on the balance and press the tare button to zero the
              weight. This ensures the balance reads only the mass of the NaCl.
   5. Weighing NaCl:
          o Using a clean, dry spatula, carefully add NaCl to the container.
          o Add the NaCl gradually to avoid exceeding 9g and adjust until the balance reads
              exactly 9.00g.
   6. Post-Weighing Precautions:
          o Close the NaCl container tightly after use to prevent contamination or spillage.
          o Transfer the NaCl to the designated area or experimental setup promptly and
              safely.
   7. Cleaning and Final Check:
          o Clean the spatula, weighing container, and the surrounding area to maintain
              laboratory hygiene.
          o Recheck the balance for any residual material and ensure it is reset for the next
              use.

By following these steps, the student ensures precise measurement while maintaining safety and
laboratory standards.

Q. No. 2: Why are micropipettes and Glass filters used in analytical
chemistry?

Answer:

   1. Micropipettes:
         o Purpose: Micropipettes are used to measure and transfer very small, precise
             volumes of liquids (typically in microliters).
         o Significance: They ensure accuracy and repeatability, making them essential for
             experiments that require precise liquid handling, such as preparing solutions,
             dilutions, or performing titrations in analytical chemistry.
   2. Glass Filters:
         o Purpose: Glass filters are used for filtration to separate fine particles or impurities
             from liquids or gases.
         o Significance: They are chemically resistant, ensuring they do not react with the
             substances being filtered. They are ideal for applications requiring high purity and
             precision, such as sample preparation or analysis in analytical chemistry.

Q. No. 3: How many significant figures are in each of the following
measurements, Convert each measurement to

Its equivalent scientific notation or decimal form.

• 0.0120 mol HCl

• 605.3 mg CaCO3

• 1.043 × 10–4 mol Ag+

• 9.3 × 104 mg NaOH

1. 0.0120 mol HCl
a) Significant Figures:

- Leading zeros are not significant

- Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant

- Therefore, 0.0120 has 3 significant figures (1,2,0)

b) Scientific Notation:

   •   0.0120 = 1.20 × 10⁻² mol HCl

2. 605.3 mg CaCO₃

a) Significant Figures:

- All non-zero digits are significant

- The decimal point determines the last significant digit

- Therefore, 605.3 has 4 significant figures (6,0,5,3)

b) Scientific Notation:

   •   605.3 = 6.053 × 10² mg CaCO₃

3. 1.043 × 10⁻⁴ mol Ag⁺

a) Significant Figures:

- All non-zero digits are significant

- Zeros between non-zero digits are significant

- Therefore, 1.043 has 4 significant figures (1,0,4,3)

b) Decimal Form:

   •   1.043 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.0001043 mol Ag⁺

4. 9.3 × 10⁴ mg NaOH

a) Significant Figures:

- All non-zero digits are significant

- Therefore, 9.3 has 2 significant figures (9,3)

b) Decimal Form:

   •   9.3 × 10⁴ = 93,000 mg NaOH

Title: Spectroscopic Analysis of Iron (Fe²⁺) in Water Samples
Introduction
Iron is an essential micronutrient found in water sources either as ferrous (Fe²⁺) or ferric (Fe³⁺) ions. However, excessive iron concentrations can cause environmental, health, and industrial issues such as staining, unpleasant taste, and damage to water systems. Hence, accurate detection of Fe²⁺ ions in water is crucial for environmental monitoring and public health.
This assignment proposes UV-Visible Spectroscopy as the primary analytical approach for the quantification of Fe²⁺ ions in water, with a justification rooted in the analyte’s chemical behavior, sensitivity requirements, and cost-effectiveness.

Selection of Spectroscopic Technique: UV-Visible Spectroscopy
1. Principle of UV-Visible Spectroscopy
UV-Visible spectroscopy relies on the absorption of ultraviolet or visible light by analyte molecules, resulting in electronic transitions. Fe²⁺ itself is not strongly absorbing; however, it can form a colored complex with certain chromogenic ligands, which makes UV-Vis a suitable method when combined with color development reagents.
2. Complexation with 1,10-Phenanthroline
For Fe²⁺ detection, the most commonly used chromogenic reagent is 1,10-phenanthroline, which forms a stable, orange-red complex with Fe²⁺ ions. This complex has a strong absorbance peak at 510 nm, making it highly suitable for UV-Vis analysis.

Justification for UV-Visible Spectroscopy
1. Specificity and Selectivity
The Fe²⁺–1,10-phenanthroline complex is specific to ferrous ions and does not form with Fe³⁺ unless pre-reduced. This makes the method selective when the goal is to measure Fe²⁺ exclusively.
2. Sensitivity
UV-Vis spectroscopy provides good sensitivity in the range of 0.1 to 5.0 mg/L for Fe²⁺ ions, aligning with WHO guidelines for drinking water iron limits (0.3 mg/L). The method can detect even trace concentrations in environmental samples.
3. Simplicity and Cost-Effectiveness
Compared to techniques like atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), UV-Vis spectroscopy is affordable, easier to use, and requires less sample preparation, especially beneficial in field labs or resource-limited settings.
4. Rapid Analysis and Quantification
UV-Vis instruments offer rapid absorbance measurements, and using Beer–Lambert’s Law, the Fe²⁺ concentration can be quickly determined based on calibration curves.

Alternative Spectroscopic Approaches: A Comparative Note
    • AAS (Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy): While AAS is more sensitive and selective for metal ion quantification, it is also more expensive and requires specialized infrastructure, making it less feasible for routine testing.
    • ICP-OES or ICP-MS: These methods provide multi-element analysis and extremely low detection limits but are cost-intensive and best suited for advanced trace-level analysis in research labs.
Given the moderate detection requirement and environmental setting, UV-Visible spectroscopy remains the most appropriate choice.

Sample Analysis Protocol
    1. Sample Collection: Water is filtered and acidified to pH <2 to stabilize iron ions.
    2. Reduction: If total iron is to be measured, Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ using hydroxylamine hydrochloride.
    3. Color Development: Add 1,10-phenanthroline reagent and buffer to maintain pH ~3.5.
    4. Spectral Measurement: Measure absorbance at 510 nm after 10 minutes.
    5. Quantification: Compare sample absorbance to a standard calibration curve prepared using known Fe²⁺ concentrations.

The proposed UV-Visible spectroscopic method for Fe²⁺ determination in water is justified based on its affordability, simplicity, and adequate sensitivity for routine environmental analysis. By forming a specific colored complex with 1,10-phenanthroline, Fe²⁺ can be accurately quantified in various aqueous matrices, helping in water quality control and environmental safety monitoring.

﻿Topic 67: Chromatography-VI
    1. INTRODUCTION
Electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate DNA, RNA, or protein molecules based on their size and electrical charge. An electric current is used to move molecules to be separated through a gel. Pores in the gel work like a sieve, allowing smaller molecules to move faster than larger molecules.

 Electrophoresis may be of two types;
    • Slab electrophoresis-TLC
    • Capillary electrophoresis-Column
    • Velocity (v) of charged molecule in an electric field can be assessed with formula;
    • 			v = Eq/F
    • where E is applied electric charge, q is net charge on a molecule, and F is frictional coefficient depends upon mass and shape of molecule.
          1.1. Identification through staining
Identification can be achieved by staining. A group of dyes allow us to visualize the paths that the particles take. From there, we can capture images to document results. Several choices exist for staining nucleic acids during gel electrophoresis.
 Two dimensional Electrophoresis
    • This technique combines two techniques; one separate the mixture of proteins according to charges (IEF) and second with the size (SDS-PAGE).
        ◦ Stationary phases:  Starch gel, PAGE (poly acrylamide gel), Agarose, Cellulose acetate
SDS-PAGE (polyacrylamide gel as a support medium and sodium dodecyl sulfate to denature the proteins)
IEF: Isoelectric focusing using agarose or polyacrylamide
        ◦ Mobile phase: Buffer system
Phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), Tris-Borate-EDTA buffer (TBE, pH 8.0), Tris-Cotrate EDTA buffer (TCE, pH 7.0), Tris-Maleic acid-EDTA buffer (TME, pH 7.5), Tris-Acetate EDTA buffer (TAE, pH 8.0), Tris glycerin buffer (TG, pH 8.5), Lithium Borate buffer (LB, pH 8.6)
Identification through staining systems
        ◦ For Proteins
General: Coomassie brillient blue R, Kenacid blue, Amido black
Specific: Oil red O, PAS (Periodic acid Schiff), Rubeanic acid, Transferrin-specific & for calcium binding proteins
        ◦ Allozyme: Histochemical staining
        ◦ DNA: EtBr (Ethedium bromide), SyBR green, Propidium iodide and silver staining
        ◦ Steps: fixing, staining, destaining

Topic 68: Chromatography-VII
    1. INTRODUCTION
High-performance liquid chromatography, formerly referred to as high-pressure liquid chromatography, is a technique in analytical chemistry used to separate, identify, and quantify each component in a mixture. HPLC is extremely quick and efficient. It uses a pump, rather than gravity, to force a liquid solvent through a solid adsorbent material, with different chemical components separating out as they move at different speeds.
The separation principle of HPLC is based on the distribution of the analyte (sample) between a mobile phase (eluent) and a stationary phase (packing material of the column). Depending on the chemical structure of the analyte, the molecules are retarded while passing the stationary phase.

Following detectors are used in HPLC:
    • UV Detector: for coloured or UV active compounds
    • PDA detector: UV based scanning
    • RI: Refractive Index detector for polysacharides
    • ELSD: Evaporating light scattering detector
    • Conductivity: for charged containing molecules
High Performance Liquid Chromatograph
    • It is normally used as reversed phase chromatographic technique
    • Mobile phase is pumped into the column with high pressure
    • Separation occur based on size, charge, affinity etc
Topic 69: Chromatography-VIII
    1. INTRODUCTION
Size exclusion HPLC columns are used primarily for the separation of proteins and carbohydrates. Other types of HPLC columns include affinity, ion exclusion, and displacement chromatography columns; a chiral HPLC column can be used to resolve racemic mixtures.
The reversed-phase HPLC column is the most versatile and commonly used column type and can be used for a wide range of different types of analytes. Normal-phase HPLC columns have polar packing. The mobile phase is nonpolar and therefore usually an organic solvent such as hexane or methylene chloride.
HPLC Columns:
    • Silica-based reversed-phase columns are stable in pH range 2-8.
    • Columns containing porous graphite or particles of polymeric materials such as styrene–divinylbenzene copolymer are stable over a wider pH range.

    1. INTRODUCTION
Electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate DNA, RNA, or protein molecules based on their size and electrical charge. An electric current is used to move molecules to be separated through a gel. Pores in the gel work like a sieve, allowing smaller molecules to move faster than larger molecules.

 Electrophoresis may be of two types;
    • Slab electrophoresis-TLC
    • Capillary electrophoresis-Column
    • Velocity (v) of charged molecule in an electric field can be assessed with formula;
    • 			v = Eq/F
    • where E is applied electric charge, q is net charge on a molecule, and F is frictional coefficient depends upon mass and shape of molecule.
          1.1. Identification through staining
Identification can be achieved by staining. A group of dyes allow us to visualize the paths that the particles take. From there, we can capture images to document results. Several choices exist for staining nucleic acids during gel electrophoresis.

Topic 68: Chromatography-VII
    1. INTRODUCTION
High-performance liquid chromatography, formerly referred to as high-pressure liquid chromatography, is a technique in analytical chemistry used to separate, identify, and quantify each component in a mixture. HPLC is extremely quick and efficient. It uses a pump, rather than gravity, to force a liquid solvent through a solid adsorbent material, with different chemical components separating out as they move at different speeds.
The separation principle of HPLC is based on the distribution of the analyte (sample) between a mobile phase (eluent) and a stationary phase (packing material of the column). Depending on the chemical structure of the analyte, the molecules are retarded while passing the stationary phase.

Following detectors are ude in HPLC:
    • UV Detector: for coloured or UV active compounds
    • PDA detector: UV based scanning
    • RI: Refractive Index detector for polysacharides
    • ELSD: Evaporating light scattering detector
    • Conductivity: for charged containing molecules
High Performance Liquid Chromatograph
    • It is normally used as reversed phase chromatographic technique
    • Mobile phase is pumped into the column with high pressure
    • Separation occur based on size, charge, affinity etc

    1. INTRODUCTION
Size exclusion HPLC columns are used primarily for the separation of proteins and carbohydrates. Other types of HPLC columns include affinity, ion exclusion, and displacement chromatography columns; a chiral HPLC column can be used to resolve racemic mixtures.
The reversed-phase HPLC column is the most versatile and commonly used column type and can be used for a wide range of different types of analytes. Normal-phase HPLC columns have polar packing. The mobile phase is nonpolar and therefore usually an organic solvent such as hexane or methylene chloride.
